name: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
intent: Let an app act on a user's data at another service without ever seeing the user's password, and, with OpenID Connect, learn who signed in.
scenario: A photo-printing app, PrintShop, asks to read a user's photos from a photo service. The user signs in and consents at the photo service, PrintShop receives a short-lived authorization code, and exchanges it for tokens. A malicious app on the same phone tries to steal the code.
problem: Before OAuth, an app that wanted your photos asked for your photo-service password. It then held full, permanent access to the whole account, could not be limited to reading photos, and could only be cut off by changing the password for every app at once. Worse, every such app became a place where the password could leak. The service needs a way to say: this specific app may do this specific thing, for a while, and the user can take it back, without the app ever touching the credential.

howItWorks.title: Four roles, and the password stays with one of them
howItWorks.text: The resource owner (the user) owns the photos. The client (PrintShop) wants access. The authorization server (login, consent, tokens) decides. The resource server (the Photo API) holds the data and accepts tokens. Often the last two are one company, but they are separate jobs. The password is typed only into the authorization server, in the user's browser, never into the client.

howItWorks.title: Authorization code flow with PKCE: front channel, then back channel
howItWorks.text: With PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange), the client invents a random code_verifier (43 to 128 characters) and sends code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)) with code_challenge_method=S256 in the /authorize request, together with response_type=code, client_id, an exact redirect_uri, scope, and a random state. After login and consent the server redirects the browser to redirect_uri?code=...&state=.... That redirect is the front channel: anyone who can see the URL sees the code. The client then calls POST /token directly (the back channel) with the code and the code_verifier. The server hashes the verifier and compares it with the stored challenge, so a stolen code is useless without the verifier, which never travelled through the browser.

howItWorks.title: Redirect URI and state are the other two locks
howItWorks.text: The server must compare redirect_uri to a registered value by exact string match (RFC 9700 forbids prefix and wildcard matching, except for the port of a localhost redirect in native apps), otherwise an open redirect (a page that forwards visitors to any URL it is given) on the client's domain forwards the code to an attacker. The client must generate an unguessable state, bind it to the user's session, and reject any callback whose state differs, which stops an attacker from injecting their own code into a victim's session (login CSRF, tricking a browser into sending a request it did not mean to). Codes are single use and live for about a minute; reuse should also revoke the tokens issued from the code.

howItWorks.title: Scopes, access tokens and refresh tokens
howItWorks.text: Consent grants scopes (openid, photos.read). The token response carries an access_token (a bearer token: whoever holds it can use it; typically 5 to 60 minutes, opaque or a JWT, a signed token), expires_in, and optionally a refresh_token (days to months) that only the client sends to the token endpoint to get new access tokens without bothering the user. The Photo API checks the signature or introspects the token, the audience, the expiry and that the scope covers the request. A leaked access token is limited by its lifetime and scope; a refresh token should be rotated on use (and the family revoked if an old one reappears) or sender-constrained.

howItWorks.title: OpenID Connect: OAuth says what you may do, OIDC says who you are
howItWorks.text: OAuth alone gives the client a key to an API, not a statement about who the user is. OpenID Connect adds the openid scope and an ID token, a signed JWT with iss, sub (a stable user id), aud (must equal the client_id), exp and the nonce the client sent (a one-time random value that ties the ID token to this request). The client validates the signature against the issuer's JWKS and checks iss, aud, exp and nonce. The userinfo endpoint returns more claims (name, email) for an access token with the right scopes. Other grants: client_credentials for machine-to-machine (no user, the client authenticates with a secret or key and gets a token for itself) and the device flow for TVs and CLIs (the device shows a code, the user approves on a phone).

pros: The app never sees the password, so a compromised app cannot leak it, and the user can sign in with MFA or passkeys without the app supporting them
Access is scoped, time-limited and revocable per app, instead of all or nothing
One identity provider serves many apps (single sign-on) through OpenID Connect
A mature standard with libraries, certified implementations and a security BCP (RFC 9700) that closes most known holes
cons: Many moving parts (redirects, state, PKCE, nonce, token validation); each skipped check is a real vulnerability
Bearer access tokens work for whoever holds them, so storage and transport matter
Revoking an already issued self-contained JWT before it expires needs extra machinery (short lifetimes, introspection, deny lists)
Needs a real authorization server (or a hosted one) to run, patch and monitor, and the login pages are now your phishing target
whenToUse: A third-party app needs delegated access to a user's data in your service
Sign in with an existing identity provider (Google, Microsoft, corporate SSO) through OpenID Connect
Many first-party apps and APIs that should share one login and one place for consent and token policy
Service-to-service calls where you want short-lived, scoped credentials (client credentials) instead of static API keys
whenNotToUse: One server-rendered app with its own users and no third parties: a session cookie on a plain login form is simpler and has fewer ways to go wrong
A single backend calling another you own: mutual TLS or a workload identity is usually enough
As a way to authenticate users with plain OAuth: an access token is not proof of login, so use OpenID Connect and validate the ID token
When you would be hand-writing the authorization server for a small product: use a maintained product or library instead
pitfalls: Using the access token as proof of who the user is: a token issued to a different app, or for a different user, passes naive checks. Validate the ID token (aud, iss, nonce) instead
Matching redirect_uri by prefix or wildcard, or having an open redirect on a registered domain: the code leaks, and PKCE does not help when the attacker started the flow themselves
Skipping PKCE because the client is confidential, or letting the server accept requests without a code_challenge, which allows a downgrade
No state check (or a state not tied to the session), which allows login CSRF: the victim ends up signed in to the attacker's account
Still using the implicit flow (tokens in the URL fragment: they land in history, referrers and logs) or the password grant; both were removed in OAuth 2.1
Keeping tokens in localStorage, where any XSS reads them; prefer a backend that holds the tokens and gives the browser an HttpOnly, SameSite cookie
Requesting broad scopes up front, long-lived non-rotating refresh tokens, and not checking the audience at the resource server

roles.label: Resource owner
roles.description: The user, in their browser, who owns the photos and approves access.

roles.label: Client
roles.description: PrintShop, the app that wants access. Public (phone, SPA) or confidential (server with a secret).

roles.label: Authorization server
roles.description: Authenticates the user, asks for consent, and issues codes and tokens.

roles.label: Resource server
roles.description: The Photo API. Validates the access token and its scope on every call.

roles.label: Attacker
roles.description: A malicious app on the same phone that registered the same URL scheme.

quiz.question: A mobile photo app uses the authorization code flow with PKCE. A malicious app on the same phone has registered the same custom URL scheme and captures the code from the redirect. It calls the token endpoint with that code. Why does the exchange fail?
options: The code is valid for only about a minute, so the attacker is always too slow to use it
It lacks the code_verifier, which never travelled through the browser redirect
The state value in the redirect does not match, so the server rejects the request
It cannot present the client secret that the real app embeds in its binary
quiz.explanation: PKCE binds the code to a random secret that only the real app knows and that never travels through the browser. A one-minute lifetime is easily beaten by an attacker already on the phone. State is checked by the client, not the server, and a mobile app cannot keep a secret.

quiz.question: A team lets users sign in with an identity provider by accepting the access token sent from a mobile app and treating its sub claim as the logged-in user. The signature and expiry check out. An attacker runs a quiz app, collects tokens from users who sign in there, and replays them to the team's API to log in as those users. What was missing?
options: The access token signature should be verified against the issuer's published keys
The access tokens should have a much shorter lifetime, such as five minutes
The callback endpoint should be served over HTTPS only
Sign in with the ID token and check that its aud equals your client_id
quiz.explanation: An access token says what a client may do, not that the user signed in to your app. Tokens issued to the quiz app pass signature and expiry checks, and a short lifetime only narrows the replay window. The aud claim of an ID token proves it was issued for your client.

quiz.question: A client registers https://app.example.com/callback. The authorization server accepts any redirect_uri that starts with https://app.example.com/. That site has an open redirect at /go?url=. An attacker builds an authorize link with redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/go?url=https://evil.test, using their own PKCE verifier, and sends it to a victim who approves. Which fix closes the hole?
options: Compare redirect_uri to the registered value by exact string match
Require PKCE on every request so a stolen code cannot be exchanged
Cut the code lifetime to a few seconds so it expires before it is misused
Require a state parameter that the client checks on the callback
quiz.explanation: With prefix matching the code is sent to the attacker, who started the flow and so holds the matching verifier, so PKCE does not help. Exact matching stops the redirect from being accepted at all. A short lifetime does not stop a fast attacker, and state is checked only by the legitimate client.
